title: How Sure Are You
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This article explains why human memory is far less reliable than confidence in it would suggest, and why that matters for leaders who rely on their recollection of events. It walks through the mechanics of memory reconstruction: because we retain only fragments of any experience, each act of recalling it involves filling gaps with plausible detail, and repeated retelling entrenches those reconstructions as if they were fact. The counterintuitive finding at the piece's center is that confidence in a memory doesn't correlate with its accuracy — if anything, the more polished and confident a memory feels, the more likely it has been embellished. The essay recommends seeking objective references to check memories that matter and dialing back the certainty leaders project when recounting events.
points: The essay's central counterintuitive claim is that confidence in a memory is not a reliable proxy for its accuracy, and may even correlate with more embellishment.
It explains the mechanism precisely: each retelling of an event forces gap-filling, and repeated retelling entrenches the reconstruction as though it were the original memory.
It offers a concrete mitigation — seeking objective references (recordings, documents, others' accounts) — for memories that matter to performance decisions.
The Kettering quote at the close crystallizes the practical risk: false certainty, not ignorance, is what gets leaders into trouble.
quotes: People are full of false memories. The reason is not because of bias or faulty thinking. It’s just because our memories are incomplete.
As soon as we reconstruct this history, we form a more complete but less accurate memory.
Here's the kicker: It seems the more we are sure of a memory, the more likely it is to be flawed. Our confidence doesn’t correlate with accuracy.

Objective references such as falsely remembering quotations, misremembering passages in books, and viewing a video of what occurred and realizing we have misremembered are always a shock to the system.
It ain’t the things you don’t know that’ll get you in trouble, but the things you know for sure that ain’t so.
